fields.meta_title: What Is the Church? The Body of Christ Explained
fields.description: The church is not a building but a people — the body of Christ, the family of God, and the bride he died to win. Here is what the Bible says the church is, and why you need it.
fields.body_html:
Ask most people what the church is and they will point to a building — a steeple, a set of pews, an hour on Sunday. But in the Bible the church is never a building; it is a people. The word itself means “those who are called out” — the whole company of people God has called out of the world to belong to himself through Jesus Christ. The church is not somewhere you go; it is something you are, together with everyone else who belongs to Christ. And Scripture piles up image after image to describe it: a body, a family, a temple, a bride, a flock, a nation. Each one reveals something about what this called-out people is meant to be.

So what is the church, really, and why does it matter so much to God? Here is what the Bible says — a vision far greater and warmer than a building could ever hold.

The church is the body of Christ

The most striking picture is that the church is a body — living, connected, and animated by one life. “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12). Every believer is a member of this body, given a place and a purpose within it, and Christ himself is the head: “he is the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18).

This image tells us two things at once. First, we belong to one another — an isolated Christian is as unnatural as a severed hand. “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Second, we need one another; no member can say to another, “I have no need of you.” The eye needs the hand, the head needs the feet. God has arranged his people so that each supplies what the others lack, and the whole grows healthy only as “each part is working properly” (Ephesians 4:16). The church is not an audience of spectators but a body of members, each one necessary.

The church is God’s family and household

The church is also a family — and this transforms how we see one another. Through Christ we are no longer strangers but “members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). God is our Father, Christ our elder brother, and every other believer our brother or sister. The bonds of this new family run deeper than blood, for they are forged by the Spirit and will outlast the grave.

This is why the New Testament is full of “one another” commands — love one another, bear one another’s burdens, forgive one another, encourage one another. These are family duties, and they are impossible to practise alone. The church is where an orphaned world is given a home, where the lonely are set in families, and where people who share nothing in common but Christ discover that in him they share everything. There is no other society on earth quite like it, where the only entrance fee is need and the bond is thicker than blood. To join the church is to be adopted into the largest and oldest family on earth.

The church is built on Christ and indwelt by his Spirit

The church is not a human society that people invented; it is a building God is constructing, with Christ as the foundation and cornerstone. Believers are “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone,” growing together “into a holy temple in the Lord” and “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:20–22). The astonishing claim is that the living God dwells not in temples of stone but in his people — collectively, they are the place where he lives on earth.

Jesus founded this church himself and pledged its indestructibility: “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). Note whose church it is — my church — and who does the building. Empires have risen and fallen, persecutions have raged, and still the church stands, because its survival does not rest on human strength but on the promise of her Lord. She is his possession, bought with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and he will not lose her.

What the church is for

God did not call the church out of the world merely to keep it safe, but to give it a mission and a purpose. The first believers show us the pattern: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). Here are the church’s core activities — the teaching of God’s word, shared fellowship, the Lord’s Supper, and prayer. Around these the church gathers, is fed, and grows.

But the church also exists to display God’s glory and declare his praise to the world. Peter gives believers a breathtaking identity: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). The church is God’s showcase — the community through which a watching world is meant to see what he is like. And gifted leaders are given “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12), so that the whole body matures into the likeness of its head.

The church is the bride Christ loves

Of all the images, none is more tender than this: the church is the bride of Christ, and he loves her as a husband loves his wife. “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her... so that he might present the church to himself in splendor” (Ephesians 5:25–27). The church is not merely an institution Christ founded; she is the beloved for whom he died, whom he is even now making beautiful, and whom he will one day present to himself radiant and without flaw.

This should reshape how we regard the church, warts and all. To despise the church is to slight the bride Christ died to win. Yes, she is still imperfect, full of flawed and forgiven sinners; but she is the object of the deepest love in the universe, and she is destined for glory. The One who began this good work in her will complete it, and the story of the church ends not in decline but at a wedding.

It also gives us patience with the church as we actually find her. Many people are wounded or disappointed by churches and conclude they are better off alone. The hurt is often real, and the church’s failures are not to be excused. But a family is not abandoned because some of its members are difficult, and a bride still loved by her husband is not to be scorned by his friends. The church on earth is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints; we come to it not because we or others have arrived, but because here the sick are being healed by the Great Physician. To love the church is not to pretend she is perfect, but to love what Christ loves, and to labour, as he does, for the day she is presented without spot.

Why you need the church — and it needs you

All of this means the Christian life was never designed to be lived alone. Some today imagine they can follow Jesus privately, without his people, but the New Testament knows nothing of a churchless Christian. We are commanded to keep meeting together: “let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together... but encouraging one another” (Hebrews 10:24–25). We grow, are guarded, and are useful only in the fellowship of the body.

So do not settle for watching from the edges. Find a church where Christ is preached and his people love one another, and throw in your lot with them — not as a consumer but as a member, giving as well as receiving. You have a place in the body that no one else can fill, and gifts the family needs. The hand cannot serve the body from a distance, and a coal removed from the fire soon grows cold; we were made to be joined to the others, warming and being warmed. The church is imperfect because it is full of people like us; but it is also the dwelling place of God, the family of the redeemed, and the bride of Christ — and there is no following Jesus apart from the people he loved enough to die for. Belong to them, and you will find you belong to him more deeply too — for it is often in the faces of his people that we see most clearly the love of the Head who binds them into one.
